newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian shares edge down, market seen quiet.
newsitem.headline: Russian shares edge down, market seen quiet.

text.p: Leading Russian shares eased in early trade after an initial jump at opening, and traders said First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais's announcement that the 1997 budget would not be fulfilled would rein in prices.

"Everything is low. There was a lot of weakness going to the close yesterday... and the news about Chubais just put a damper on the entire complex," said Peter Kizenko, chief equities trader at ING Barings.
The Russian Trading System 23-share index opened almost unchanged on at 298.82 after closing on Wednesday at 298.81.

Market leader UES fell to $0.2142 at 0835 GMT from an early $0.2161 after closing on Wednesday at $0.2135 and oil producer LUKoil fell to $13.450 after jumping to $13.580 at opening and closing on Wednesday at $13.400.
Other dealers said volumes were low but said Chubais's budget announcement, only the latest in a series of government admissions of low tax collection rates, was only incidental to sluggish trade.
"It's clear there's a downward correction on the market and people are waiting until they see some stabilisation," said Igor Lossavio, head of overseas trading at Prospekt.
He said investors were turning to lower-tier shares.
"There's very picky investment in the third and fourth tiers. People are looking to undervalued companies," said Lossavio.
Regional power utility Mosenergo nosed higher to $1.217 from $1.215.

But dealers said the annual Mosenergo shareholders' meeting on Monday, at which charter amendments unfavourable to foreign investors are expected to be approved, could drive company shares and the market overall lower next week.
"I don't believe it's been entirely priced in yet, and if the charter amendments are passed it's going to put a damper on the entire market...This could really shock some people," said Kizenko.
But traders said they did not expect serious movement on the market today.
"The only thing I see is some short covering. After two consecutive false starts people are becoming a little bit gun-shy," said Kizenko, referring to recent short-term market rises.
